questions.q: A reporter's story opens: "The school board met Thursday night in the high-school library." What's wrong with it as an inverted-pyramid lede?
choices: It leads with background, not with what happened
It saves the scene for later instead of opening with an anecdote
It answers too many of the five Ws at once
It should end with a kicker that circles back
questions.explain: A summary lede leads with the news. A meeting happening isn't news; what the board decided is.

questions.q: How does the inverted pyramid order its material?
choices: By rising tension, toward a climax
In the order events happened
From a specific person to the general issue and back
By importance, most important first
questions.explain: It orders facts by importance, which is why it doesn't map onto the dramatic arc.

questions.q: Why can an editor cut an inverted-pyramid story from the bottom without rewriting?
choices: The ending always repeats the lede
The nut graf carries all the meaning
Each paragraph is less essential than the one before
The last paragraph is reserved for quotes, which are optional
questions.explain: Because importance falls as the story goes on, the end holds the least essential material.

questions.q: What's the most accurate thing to say about the popular telegraph explanation of the form's origin?
choices: It is proven by Civil War dispatches
Historians doubt it caused the form: chronological stories persisted long after the telegraph
It was invented by Tom Wolfe as a joke
It is accurate, but only for British newspapers
questions.explain: The telegraph may have helped, but historians point to other causes, such as official dispatches, wire services and the ideal of objectivity.

questions.q: A magazine wants a long piece that readers will finish, about a family's year-long fight with an insurer that has just ended. Is the inverted pyramid the best choice?
choices: No: a story that has resolved, meant to be read to the end, suits a narrative or feature structure
Yes, because the most important fact should always come first
Yes, because readers can stop anywhere
No: the inverted pyramid is only for sports
questions.explain: The inverted pyramid informs fast but gives readers no reason to keep going. A resolved story can carry a full narrative.

questions.q: What are the five Ws and H for?
choices: A fixed order in which every news story must present its facts
The six acts of a feature story
A method for writing kickers
A checklist so nothing essential is missing; the lede uses the ones that matter most for this event
questions.explain: They're a checklist, not a template. Which ones lead depends on the event.

questions.q: A critic says the inverted pyramid 'hides judgment'. What do they mean?
choices: Reporters hide their opinions in the kicker
The form forbids quotations
Deciding what's 'most important' is a choice, and what gets put at the bottom is what gets cut
Editors never read past the lede
questions.explain: The form looks neutral, but ranking facts is an editorial decision, and context at the bottom is often lost.

ideas: Put the outcome in the first sentence, so a reader who stops anywhere still has the essentials.
Order facts by importance rather than by time, so an editor can cut from the end without rewriting.
A news story's first sentence should summarize the whole event in one self-contained line.
